(Full fetch, published 13 October 2026)
Hitting the buffers
Previewing the key decisions for Autumn Budget 2026 in the context of another rise in the cost of living
            13 October 2026          
Hannah Aldridge 
Matthew Cavanagh 
Nye Cominetti 
Ruth Curtice 
Zachary Leather 
Jonathan Marshall 
Cillian Sheehan 
James Smith 
This briefing note previews the key decisions facing the Chancellor at Autumn Budget 2026. It assesses how the economic backdrop is likely to affect the OBR’s fiscal forecasts, and sets out how the Government should respond to the twin challenges of another rise in the cost of living and stretched public finances.
The UK economy has been more resilient than expected, growing by 1.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, the fastest rate in the G7. But conflict in the Middle East has once again pushed up energy prices and interest rates. Household energy bills are expected to rise to around £2,000 from January, close to the peak reached after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. At the same time, higher borrowing costs mean we estimate debt interest spending will be higher in 2029-30 than forecast in March, halving the Chancellor’s headroom to £12 billion.
The Government appears to want a low-key Budget, but two challenges cannot be ducked. With little scope for extra borrowing, cost of living support must be targeted and temporary, focused on families struggling to heat their homes or pay rent. And the Chancellor should rebuild headroom to at least £20 billion, keeping a tight grip on spending and raising around £8 billion from tax reforms that also improve the system.
Key findings
Higher government borrowing costs will push debt interest spending around £14 billion above the OBR’s forecast in 2029-30.
Taking everything together, we estimate that headroom against the Government’s fiscal target will be halved, from £24 billion to £12 billion.
The typical family is £2,900 worse off than if the economy had behaved as expected before the pandemic, and almost one-in-five households in the poorest half of the country are already behind on priority bills.
Housing support for private renters on low incomes has been frozen since April 2024 while rents have risen by more than 20 per cent, leaving a family renting a typical two-bedroom home facing a shortfall of nearly £160 a month.
Recommendations
Provide a temporary discount on energy prices for households where no individual has an income above £24,000, costing £2 billion this year and worth an average of £175 per eligible household. If this cannot be delivered by January, increase the Warm Home Discount and top up the Crisis and Resilience Fund instead
Permanently relink Local Housing Allowance to the 30
th
 percentile of local rents, at a cost of £2.3 billion in 2029-30. This could be funded from within the existing working-age welfare budget through an increase to the Universal Credit taper rate.
Rebuild headroom to at least £20 billion by sticking to existing cash spending plans and raising around £8 billion in tax: for example, by ending Capital Gains Tax exemptions on death and on leaving the UK, lowering the VAT registration threshold, and charging National Insurance on partnership income.
End the freeze on Fuel Duty, with small, predictable increases.
